newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strikes, Hanbo woes batter South Korean economy.
newsitem.headline: Strikes, Hanbo woes batter South Korean economy.

text.p: Hanbo Steel Co's financial failure and labour strife are forcing economists to scale down forecasts for the South Korean economy, and some said on Thursday the growth this year could be the weakest since 1980.
The economists said the nation's gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast was being lowered to between five and six percent in 1997 against estimated growth of 6.9 percent in 1996.

"We've revised the 1997 GDP growth forecast to 5.0 percent from 6.3 percent due to the labour strikes and Hanbo crisis," said Hong Sun-young, a senior economist at Samsung Economic Research Institute.
The projected growth is the lowest since 1980 when GDP shrunk by 2.7 percent.
"The Hanbo scandal and the strikes aggravated the already depressed economy," said Hong.
More than three weeks of industrial strife hit some of the country's export industry in January, pushing the trade deficit to a monthly record of $3.48 billion.
Stoppages began on December 26 when the ruling party rammed a new labour law through parliament to make it easier for companies to sack workers and replace strikers.
The strikes cost the nation 2.85 trillion won ($3.28 billion) in lost production and $509 million in lost exports.
The automobile industry was hit hardest, with an output loss totalling 2.39 trillion won and an export loss $369.9 million.
"Exports had been the engine behind South Korea's economy," said Park Kwang-soo, an economist at Ssangyong Economic Research Institute. "Now the engine is sputtering."
He said the Japanese yen's fall versus the dollar would continue to hammer exports. The yen's weakness would make Japanese products more competitive against South Korean goods.
Economists said the labour strife could re-emerge later this month when workers begin wage negotiations with management, thus further depressing already sluggish corporate investment.

Lee Yong-man, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute said strikes have also discouraged companies from investing in plants. "Many are delaying investment plans until the economy shows some sign of improvement."
Fallouts from insolvent Hanbo Steel Co, the nation's second largest steelmaker and flagship of Hanbo Group, could deal a brutal blow to small businesses.
Hanbo defaulted on debt repayments on January 23 after accumulating five trillion won in loans.
Economists said Hanbo's trouble would force banks to be more cautious in providing loans, making it difficult for small companies to borrow. Some could be forced into bankruptcies, they said.
"It's a psychological depression which is a bigger problem," said Lee of LG. "A sense of crisis has prevailed in the society, cooling private consumption and corporate investment."
Lee Keun-mo, research head at ING-Barings Securities said the worst was expected in the first quarter.
"The economy is seen growing a mere four percent in the first quarter and less than six percent for the whole year."
